title: V&A East Storehouse: the museum that shows its workings
seo_title: V&A East Storehouse: What to See and Know
description: An independent guide to V&A East Storehouse in Hackney Wick: what makes it different, what to notice and how to plan a worthwhile visit.
dek: Half a million objects, open storage and a museum that lets the backstage machinery become part of the visit. The scale is striking; the freedom to follow your own curiosity is the real point.
body:
V&A East Storehouse does not behave like a conventional museum. There is no prescribed sequence of galleries and no attempt to make the collection look finished. Instead, the building exposes the storage systems, conservation work and unlikely neighbours that normally sit behind the public face of a museum.

That distinction matters. The first impression is architectural — a cavernous hall, industrial shelving and objects visible across several levels — but the more interesting change is editorial. You are not being led through a single argument. You are being invited to notice connections for yourself.

## A collection store that visitors can actually enter

The Storehouse opened in 2025 at Here East, on the western edge of Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. It holds more than 500,000 objects, around 1,000 archives and hundreds of thousands of books. Those figures explain the scale, but not the experience.

The Weston Collections Hall forms the centre of the public route. Displays are set into and around the working store, mixing familiar names with objects that would struggle to justify a permanent gallery of their own. A historic interior can sit near fashion, furniture, theatre material or a fragment of architecture. The lack of a tidy hierarchy is productive: it makes the collection feel less like a textbook and more like accumulated evidence of how people make things.

This is not simply a warehouse with labels added. Sightlines, bridges and openings have been designed to make the working collection legible without pretending that every object is permanently on display. Some areas remain operational; others offer close views of large pieces that could not easily appear at South Kensington.

## What is worth slowing down for

The mistake would be to treat the building as a checklist. Its value comes from wandering, looking up and allowing one object to redirect the visit. The mini-displays around the central hall are useful starting points, but the most memorable moments may be the accidental combinations between them.

Look for changes in scale. The building can move abruptly from something monumental to a small working detail: a label, a packing support, a conservation clue or an object placed temporarily in view. These transitions reveal that museums are not neutral containers. Decisions about storage, access, interpretation and care determine what the public gets to see.

The Study Centre extends that idea. Through the V&A’s Order an Object service, material not currently on display can be requested for an appointment. The David Bowie Centre is also based here, giving the archive a permanent home while presenting changing selections from it. Both services need more planning than a casual visit, so check the current arrangements before travelling.

## How long to allow

A first visit can work in 90 minutes, but two to three hours is more realistic if you want to follow several threads without rushing. The open layout makes it easy to underestimate time: a display that looks small from the other side of the hall may contain enough detail to hold you for twenty minutes.

There is no obligation to be comprehensive. Choose a level, follow a material or subject that catches your attention, and leave something for another visit. The free admission makes repeat visits a better strategy than trying to absorb half a million objects in one afternoon.

## Getting there without turning it into a transport exercise

Hackney Wick is the most natural rail station for the Storehouse. The walk through Here East is straightforward once you are on the correct side of the canal, but this is still an area where building names and large developments can make a short route feel less obvious than it is. Check the final walking route rather than relying only on the postcode.

Stratford offers more rail and Underground connections, followed by a longer walk, local bus or the Here East shuttle when it is operating. If the weather is good, arriving through the Olympic Park can be part of the visit rather than dead time.

## Who will get the most from it

The Storehouse works particularly well for people interested in design, architecture, archives or the practical life of museums. It is also useful for repeat London visitors who have already seen the major South Kensington galleries and want a different relationship with the same collection.

It may be less satisfying for somebody who wants a short list of masterpieces and a clear route between them. The freedom is genuine, but it asks the visitor to do some of the selecting. That is not a flaw; it is the proposition.

> Come for the visible scale. Stay for the smaller realisation that every museum display is the end of a much longer chain of choices.

V&A East Storehouse is unusual not because the objects have never been seen, but because it changes what counts as the museum. Storage, research, cataloguing and conservation are no longer hidden support functions. They become part of the public experience — incomplete, sometimes overwhelming, and far more interesting for it.
